source.title: New results and open problems on subgraph centrality

accepted.question_text: Let A be a non-diagonalizable n × n matrix whose entries are nonnegative algebraic numbers, and regard A as the adjacency matrix of a weighted directed graph G. Fix an algebraic number β ≠ 0. If two vertices i and j satisfy [e^{βA}]_{ii} = [e^{βA}]_{jj}, must i and j be cospectral, meaning that [A^r]_{ii} = [A^r]_{jj} for every integer r ≥ 0? Prove this statement or provide a counterexample.

evidence.quote: Definition 2.2. Two vertices i, j of G are cospectral if for every integer r ≥ 0, [Ar]ii = [Ar]jj .

Problem 1. Let A be a (non diagonalizable) n × n matrix, whose entries are all nonnegative algebraic numbers, regarded as the adjacency matrix of a weighted directed graph G. Let β ̸= 0 be an algebraic number. Prove or disprove the following statement: if for two vertices i, j we have [eβA]ii = [eβA]jj , then i and j are cospectral.

accepted.question_text: For two vertices i and j of a graph G, let I be the set of positive real numbers β such that i and j are β-subgraph equivalent, meaning [e^{βA}]_{ii} = [e^{βA}]_{jj}. The paper proves that if I has an accumulation point, then i and j are cospectral and in fact I = R^+. Can this result be strengthened to the case where I is finite? More specifically, is there a condition on the finite cardinality M = |I| that forces i and j to be cospectral or forces I to equal all positive real numbers?

evidence.quote: Definition 2.1. Two vertices i, j of G are β-subgraph equivalent if [ eβA]ii = [eβA]jj .

Theorem 2.5. Given two vertices i, j of G, let I be the set of all β > 0 such that i and j are β-subgraph equivalent. If there is a β0 ∈ I which is an accumulation point for a sequence in I, then i and j are cospectral and I is necessarily all of R+.
It is natural to ask if this result can be improved. For example, is it still true if I is finite? Is there any condition on M = |I|, the cardinality of I, under which the result holds?

accepted.question_text: For a graph G with adjacency matrix A, define the subgraph centrality of a vertex i by SC(i, β) = [e^{βA}]_{ii}. Two non-cospectral vertices i and j interlace at β when SC(i, β) = SC(j, β); such a β is called an interlacing value. Given k ∈ N, characterize the smallest graph or graphs that contain a pair of vertices with at least k interlacing values for subgraph centrality. Conversely, for a graph on n vertices, determine the largest possible number of subgraph-centrality interlacing values that one pair of vertices can have, and in particular decide whether there are graph classes for which the general upper bound d − 1, where d is the number of distinct eigenvalues of A, is attained.
accepted.context_brief: Extremal interlacing counts for subgraph centrality

evidence.quote: the subgraph centrality is defined as follows: SC (i, β) = [ eβA]ii.
Definition 2.6. Let i, j be two non-cospectral vertices of a graph G. We say that i and j interlace at β if SC (i, β) = SC (j, β); β is an interlacing value .

Problem 2. Given k ∈ N, characterize the smallest graph(s) with a pair of vertices that have at least k interlacing values of the subgraph centrality. Conversely, given a graph with n vertices, what is the largest number of possible interlacing values for a pair of its vertices? In particular, are there classes of graphs for which the bound d − 1 is attained?

accepted.question_text: For subgraph centrality, is there a simple general construction that produces graphs with many interlacing values, meaning many positive parameters β for which a fixed pair of non-cospectral vertices i and j satisfy [e^{βA}]_{ii} = [e^{βA}]_{jj}?
accepted.context_brief: Constructing graphs with many interlacing values

evidence.quote: Definition 2.6. Let i, j be two non-cospectral vertices of a graph G. We say that i and j interlace at β if SC (i, β) = SC (j, β); β is an interlacing value .
A related, more informal problem is the following: is there a simple way to construct graphs with many interlacing values?

accepted.question_text: The paper proves that if G is a possibly weighted undirected graph with adjacency matrix A and d distinct eigenvalues, then any two non-cospectral vertices have at most d − 1 interlacing values for subgraph centrality. Does the same conclusion remain true for directed graphs, allowing positive edge weights? In other words, for a directed graph with positive weights, must every pair of non-cospectral vertices have at most d − 1 positive parameters β such that [e^{βA}]_{ii} = [e^{βA}]_{jj}?

evidence.quote: Theorem 2.9. Let G be a (possibly weighted) undirected graph with adjacency matrix A, and denote by d the number of distinct eigenvalues of A. For any two non-cospectral vertices i, j there can be at most d − 1 interlacing values for the subgraph centrality.
Problem 3. Does Theorem 2.9 hold in the case of directed graphs? (Here we allow the graph to be weighted with positive weights.)

accepted.question_text: For simple undirected graphs, the generic upper bound d − 1 on the number of subgraph-centrality interlacing values often greatly overestimates what happens in computed examples. Find sharper upper bounds for specific graph classes by exploiting structural restrictions on their 0-1 adjacency matrices, eigenvalues, or eigenvectors.

evidence.quote: In practice, we found that the bound d − 1 dramatically overestimates the typical number of interlacing values.
Obtaining sharper bounds for specific classes of graphs represents an open problem. We return on this topic in section 3.

accepted.question_text: Determine whether the examples in Figures 1 and 2 are truly minimal. More precisely, prove or disprove that the smallest graph with at least two interlacing values for exponential subgraph centrality has 9 vertices, and that the smallest graph with at least two interlacing values for resolvent centrality has 10 vertices.

evidence.quote: Figure 1: Graph with n = 9 nodes. It is the smallest graph we have found with at least two interlacing points: for vertices 2 and 8, the interlacing values are approximately β ≈ 2.12, 4.48.
Proving the minimality of these examples remains an open question.
Figure 2: Graph with n = 10 nodes. It is the smallest graph we have found with at least two interlacing values for resolvent centrality.

accepted.question_text: Let f be an admissible analytic matrix function used to define a parameter-dependent functional centrality by the diagonal entries [f(βA)]_{ii}. Under the same hypotheses that guarantee finiteness of interlacing for subgraph centrality, the paper notes that the number of interlacing points cannot be infinite. Can one prove an explicit quantitative upper bound on the number of interlacing values in terms of structural data of the graph or of the function f for such general functional centralities?

evidence.quote: Similarly to these centralities, interlacing may occur also for functional centrality. It is possible to adapt the proof of Theorem 2.7 also for this case, concluding that under the same assumptions the number of interlacing points cannot be infinite.
However, without more information on the function f , it is difficult to prove a quantitative bound on the number of interlacing values as we have done with subgraph and resolvent centralities.

accepted.question_text: For a graph G with adjacency matrix A and spectral radius ρ, the resolvent centrality of vertex i is RC(i, α) = [(I − αA)^{-1}]_{ii} for 0 < α < 1/ρ. For a fixed pair of vertices, compare the numbers of interlacing values for resolvent centrality and exponential subgraph centrality. Is it always true that the number of α for which RC(i, α) = RC(j, α) is less than or equal to the number of β for which [e^{βA}]_{ii} = [e^{βA}]_{jj}? Prove or disprove this statement.
accepted.context_brief: Comparing resolvent and subgraph interlacing counts

evidence.quote: The resolvent centrality [15] (also called resolvent subgraph centrality) with parameter α is defined as follows: RC(i, α) = [( I − αA)− 1]ii.

Problem 4. For a given pair of vertices of a graph G, prove or disprove the following statement: the number of interlacing values relative to resolvent centrality is always less than or equal to the number of interlacing values relative to subgraph centrality.
